title: Low back pain going down one leg

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi, Joanne, come on in. What can I do for you today?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's my back. Well, it's my leg, really. I've got this shooting pain going all the way down.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: When did it start?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About three weeks ago. I was lifting a resident at work and I felt something go.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What do you do for work?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a care assistant at a nursing home.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Which leg is the pain going down?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My left. No, sorry, the right. I always mix them up when I'm talking. It's definitely the right leg.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, the right. Where exactly does it go?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: From my bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of my calf and into my foot.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How bad is it, out of ten?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Seven on a bad day. Worse when I've been sitting for a while.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Is it worse in your back or your leg?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The leg, definitely.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any pins and needles or numbness in the leg?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A bit of tingling on the outside of my foot sometimes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any weakness? Tripping over your foot, anything like that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, it's just painful.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I need to ask some important questions. Any numbness around your bottom or between your legs, like when you sit on the toilet?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any change in your waterworks? Trouble passing urine, or leaking?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, that's all normal.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any problems with your bowels, or accidents?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any fevers or feeling unwell in yourself?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you ever had cancer, or lost any weight without trying?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, neither.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What have you been taking for it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ibuprofen from the supermarket, 400 three times a day. It barely touches it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any problems with your stomach, asthma or kidneys?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines, or allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No other medicines. No allergies.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Okay, let me examine you. Can you bend forward for me? That's limited by the pain. I'm going to lift your right leg up straight. Tell me when it hurts.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Ow, there. That shoots right down.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's at about 40 degrees. And the left leg?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That's fine.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Push against my hands. Pull up. Your power is normal in both legs. Your knee and ankle reflexes are normal. Can you feel me touching here? And here?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, the same on both sides.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Good. So this sounds like sciatica, where a disc in your lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg. The good news is that most of these settle over a few weeks to a couple of months.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It's really getting me down.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I understand. The ibuprofen isn't doing enough, so I'll switch you to naproxen, 500 milligrams twice a day with food, and add omeprazole, 20 milligrams once a day, to protect your stomach. Just for a couple of weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll refer you to physiotherapy. The most important thing is to keep moving as much as you can, rather than resting in bed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What about work? I can't lift people like this.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll give you a fit note for two weeks, saying you may be fit for work with amended duties, so no lifting or handling.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'd like to see you again in four weeks to see how you're getting on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Very important: if you get numbness around your bottom or genitals, difficulty passing urine, loss of control of your bladder or bowels, or weakness in both legs, go to A&E straight away. That could be a rare emergency called cauda equina syndrome. I'll give you a leaflet with these symptoms on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. I'll keep it in my purse.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Right-sided sciatica-type leg pain for 3 weeks.
reference_note.history: Onset 3 weeks ago while lifting a resident at work. Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot; leg pain worse than back pain; up to 7/10, worse after sitting. Occasional tingling over the lateral foot. No weakness. No saddle anaesthesia or change in bladder or bowel function. No fevers. No history of cancer or unintentional weight loss. Works as a care assistant.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with little benefit. No other medications. No known drug allergies. No history of peptic ulcer, asthma or renal disease.
reference_note.examination: Lumbar flexion limited by pain. Straight leg raise positive on the right at 40 degrees; negative on the left. Power, reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
reference_note.impression: Right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy. No red flags.
reference_note.plan: Stop ibuprofen. Start naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and omeprazole 20 mg once daily, for 2 weeks. Refer to physiotherapy. Advised to keep active and avoid bed rest. Fit note for 2 weeks: may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling). Review in 4 weeks.
reference_note.safety_netting: Attend A&E immediately if saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina symptoms). Symptom leaflet given.
